title: Isaiah 36:11–22
context: Please speak to your servants in Aramaic; Rabshakeh speaks Hebrew to the wall; eat dung and drink urine; do not let Hezekiah deceive you; land of bread and vineyards; the people silent as the king commanded; Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah with clothes torn. The unit stays with that historic 8th-century wall-speech—as Wesley and Calvin actually read—not a newspaper, not a millennial camp fight.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Historic words on Aramaic asked and Hebrew cried to the wall, dung and urine, Hezekiah not to deceive, the land of bread and vineyards, the people’s silence, and Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah with clothes torn—so each camp speaks in its own voice beside Isaiah 36:11–22.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: He sends Rabshakeh, who by his blasphemous persuasions tempts Hezekiah to despair, and the people to revolt. The history related here, and in the three following chapters, is, almost in the same words contained 2 Kings 18, 19, 20. It is inserted here, to explain and confirm some of the foregoing predictions. To the men—To tell them to what extremities and miseries he will force them. Jews language—The tradition of the Jews is, that Rabshaketh was an apostate Jew. If so, his ignorance of the God of Israel was the less excusable, and his enmity the less strange: for apostates are usually the most bitter and spiteful enemies. A present—Upon which terms, I will give you no disturbance; but quietly suffer each of you to enjoy his own possession. Thus saith—But what are the greatest men when they come to compare with God, or when God comes to contend with them? Is not—Thus boldly he speaks of the things which he understood not, judging of the great God, by their petty gods.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Isa 36:11–22; 2 Kgs 18:26–37)

reformed.quote: This circumstance again shews how deeply Hezekiah was depressed, when by his ambassador he entreats so humbly the servant of his enemy. They request that he will not speak in the presence of the people; because it is difficult to restrain a people naturally giddy and fickle. These ambassadors therefore gain nothing from Rabshakeh; when he is entreated, he grows worse. Rabshakeh was not sent for the purpose of offering any conditions of peace, but rather to obtain an unconditional surrender; they will perish through hunger, and will be compelled to eat and drink what is revolting. It was exceedingly shocking that the holy language, consecrated to the mysteries of heavenly wisdom, was profaned and prostituted to wicked blasphemies; no enemies are more destructive than those who speak the same language as ourselves. He calls it imposture and deception for Hezekiah to rely on his favor. Wicked men, though they assert the power of God, treat it with contempt; we must adhere firmly to the promises, that, hoping against hope, we may trust in God. He invites them to pleasures, that they may forget God; he makes use of the word blessing as a cloak to that bondage which was in itself hateful; to revolt from a pious king, whom God had appointed, and who was a type of Christ, was more wretched than anything else that could befall them. Peace cannot be made in any other way than by going into banishment; he cunningly passes by the worship of God, the temple, the kingdom. Now he openly insults God himself, and boasts that he will gain the victory over God. Look at these two kingdoms subdued; will your God resist me? If wicked men are more powerful, let us not think that the arm of God is broken. They were silent because they obeyed the king’s command; it is no despicable courage, even when we have it not in our power to utter a syllable, still not to shrink or flinch. They tear their garments; I except Shebna, who was destitute of piety, and was only driven by shame to assume the dress of mourning as a matter of form.

verses.text: Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Do not speak to us in the language of Judah within the hearing of the people who are on the wall.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: he sends Rabshakeh, who by his blasphemous persuasions tempts Hezekiah to despair, and the people to revolt. Aramaic asked at the wall is still that embassy trying to keep the blasphemy from the hearers on the wall.

Arminian reading: they might yet have asked for Syrian in that hour. Historic 8th-century wall-speech is already named. The church is not to hunt another tongue to make “speak to your servants in Aramaic” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: this circumstance again shews how deeply Hezekiah was depressed, when by his ambassador he entreats so humbly the servant of his enemy. They request that he will not speak in this manner in the presence of the people; because it is difficult to restrain a people naturally giddy and fickle. These ambassadors therefore gain nothing from Rabshakeh; when he is entreated, he grows worse.

Reformed note: the request is still that historic plea at the wall. Calvin will not let Aramaic become a newspaper of later diplomacies.

verses.text: But the Rabshakeh said, “Has my master sent me to speak these words to your master and to you, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are doomed with you to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: to the men—to tell them to what extremities and miseries he will force them. Dung and urine are still that threat after the Aramaic plea of v. 11.

Arminian pastoral: they might yet have heard the misery named and not taken it as the last word. Historic wall-speech, 8th century, is already named. The church is not to stretch “eat their own dung” into a later headline.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: hence we see the fierceness and insolence of the enemy. Rabshakeh was not sent for the purpose of offering any conditions of peace, but rather to obtain an unconditional surrender, and to strike the people with alarm; that they will perish through hunger, and will be compelled to eat and drink what is revolting.

Reformed accent: the dung and urine stay that historic scare at the wall. Calvin will not let the threat become a newspaper pasted onto “the men sitting on the wall.”

verses.text: Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out in a loud voice in the language of Judah: “Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria!
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: Jews language—the tradition of the Jews is, that Rabshaketh was an apostate Jew. If so, his ignorance of the God of Israel was the less excusable, and his enmity the less strange: for apostates are usually the most bitter and spiteful enemies. The loud Hebrew cry is still that spite after dung and urine in v. 12.

Arminian reading: they might yet have heard an apostate’s mouth, not the LORD’s. Historic language of Judah at that wall is already named. The church is not to hunt another shout to make “called out in a loud voice” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: it was, indeed, exceedingly shocking that the holy language, which had been consecrated to the mysteries of heavenly wisdom, was profaned and prostituted to wicked blasphemies. No enemies are more destructive than those who speak the same language as ourselves. When the Prophet says that he stood, he expresses the fierceness and insolence of the wicked man.

Reformed note: the cry is still that historic Hebrew at the wall. Calvin will not let the holy tongue’s misuse become a newspaper of later speech.
verses.keyContrast: Both keep the loud Hebrew cry as historic wall-speech, not a newspaper and not a millennial camp fight. Wesley reads the Jews’ language through the tradition that Rabshaketh was an apostate Jew; if so, his ignorance of the God of Israel was the less excusable, and his enmity the less strange, for apostates are usually the most bitter and spiteful enemies. Calvin reads the same cry as profanation: the holy language consecrated to the mysteries of heavenly wisdom was prostituted to wicked blasphemies; no enemies are more destructive than those who speak the same language as ourselves. Neither comment is an Arminian–Reformed millennial fight.

verses.text: Thus says the king: ‘Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: thus saith—but what are the greatest men when they come to compare with God, or when God comes to contend with them? “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you” is still that blasphemous persuasion tempting Hezekiah to despair, after the loud cry of v. 13.

Arminian pastoral: they might yet have measured that “great king” against God. Historic 8th-century taunt at the wall is already named. The church is not to stretch “he will not be able to deliver you” into a later headline.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: while he claims for his master the name of king, he speaks of Hezekiah as a private individual, without adding any title. He goes on to utter impudent calumnies against him, and at the same time vomits out his venom against God himself; for he calls it imposture and deception for Hezekiah to rely on his favor. Rabshakeh’s assertion, that they cannot be delivered by the hand of Hezekiah, is indeed true, unless God assist.

Reformed accent: the charge of deceit is still that historic calumny at the wall. Calvin will not let “do not let Hezekiah deceive you” become a newspaper of later kings.

verses.text: Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, “The LORD will surely deliver us. This city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s sending still holds: he sends Rabshakeh, who by his blasphemous persuasions tempts Hezekiah to despair, and the people to revolt. Trust in the LORD is still that persuasion after the deceit-charge of v. 14.

Arminian reading: they might yet have kept Hezekiah’s word and not called it a cheat. Historic promise of deliverance at that wall is already named. This is not a millennial camp fight. The church is not to hunt another city to make “the LORD will surely deliver us” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he quotes the exhortation by which Hezekiah encouraged the people, and speaks lightly of it as an idle and unfounded speech. Wicked men, though they assert the power of God, treat it with contempt. We must adhere firmly to the promises, that, hoping against hope, we may trust in God, and not suffer ourselves to be drawn away from him by any allurements.

Reformed note: the trust mocked is still Hezekiah’s historic word at the wall. Calvin will not let “trust in the LORD” become a newspaper of later hopes.

verses.text: Do not listen to Hezekiah. For thus says the king of Assyria: Make your peace with me and come out to me. Then each one of you will eat of his own vine, and each one of his own fig tree, and each one of you will drink the water of his own cistern,
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: a present—upon which terms, I will give you no disturbance; but quietly suffer each of you to enjoy his own possession. Vine, fig, and cistern are still that present after the trust-taunt of v. 15.

Arminian pastoral: they might yet have refused the present and kept the king God had set. Historic offer at the wall, 8th century, is already named. The church is not to stretch “make your peace with me” into a later headline.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: while he labors to turn away the hearts of the people from Hezekiah, he at the same time invites them to pleasures, that they may forget God. To make a blessing is to conduct themselves in a friendly manner. He makes use of the word blessing as a cloak to that bondage which was in itself hateful. To revolt from a pious king, whom God had appointed, and who was a type of Christ, was more wretched and miserable than anything else that could befall them.

Reformed accent: the vine and fig stay that historic bait at the wall. Calvin will not let the “blessing” pass as peace, nor as a newspaper of later plenty.
verses.keyContrast: Both keep the vine, fig, and cistern as that historic offer at the wall, not a newspaper and not a millennial camp fight. Wesley reads the present as terms on which he will give no disturbance, but quietly suffer each to enjoy his own possession. Calvin reads “make a blessing” as a cloak to bondage: to revolt from a pious king, whom God had appointed, and who was a type of Christ, was more wretched than anything else, and could not take place without denying God. Neither comment is an Arminian–Reformed millennial fight.

verses.text: until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s present of v. 16 still holds: upon which terms, I will give you no disturbance; but quietly suffer each of you to enjoy his own possession. The land of bread and vineyards is still that present’s second term, exile after the cistern.

Arminian reading: they might yet have seen banishment under the bread. Historic 8th-century deportation-offer is already named. The church is not to hunt another vineyard to make “a land of bread and vineyards” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he now adds another condition far harder than the former; for he declares that peace cannot be made with Sennacherib in any other way than by the people going into banishment. This was nothing else than to abandon the worship of God and degenerate into superstition, and voluntarily to quit the inheritance which God had given them. He says that the country is equally fertile and productive; yet he cunningly passes by what ought above all other things to be valued by them, the worship of God, the temple, the kingdom.

Reformed note: the bread-land is still that historic exile-promise at the wall. Calvin will not let grain and wine hide the temple, nor become a newspaper of later plenty.

verses.text: Beware lest Hezekiah mislead you by saying, “The LORD will deliver us.” Has any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: is not—thus boldly he speaks of the things which he understood not, judging of the great God, by their petty gods. “The LORD will deliver us” mocked beside the nations’ gods is still that misunderstanding after the bread-land of v. 17.

Arminian pastoral: they might yet have refused to weigh the LORD with petty gods. Historic wall-speech is already named. This is not a millennial camp fight. The church is not to stretch “gods of the nations” into a later headline.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: formerly he boasted that he was God’s servant, and that God had sent him to destroy Judea; but now he openly insults God himself. The wicked Rabshakeh bursts forth with greater violence, and boasts that he will gain the victory over God himself. Have any of the gods of the nations rescued their land? He does not hesitate to compare himself to the living God.

Reformed accent: the taunt is still that historic insult at the wall. Calvin will not let “the LORD will deliver us” be weighed with idols, nor pasted onto a newspaper.

verses.text: Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand?
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s petty gods of v. 18 still hold: thus boldly he speaks of the things which he understood not, judging of the great God, by their petty gods. Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, and Samaria are still that judgment after the nations’ gods.

Arminian reading: they might yet have seen fallen towns and not called the LORD one more name. Historic Syria and Samaria at that wall, 8th century, are already named. The church is not to hunt another Hamath to make “where are the gods” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he mentions chiefly the neighboring cities, the destruction of which might affect them more deeply on account of their being better known to the Jews. I have no doubt that these places belonged to Syria and Israel; as if he had said, Look at these two kingdoms subdued, which were presided over by their gods as their guardians. Will your God resist me?

Reformed note: Hamath and Samaria stay those historic neighbor-falls. Calvin will not let the list become a newspaper of later empires.

verses.text: Who among all the gods of these lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?’”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s petty gods still hold: thus boldly he speaks of the things which he understood not, judging of the great God, by their petty gods. Jerusalem set beside those lands is still that blasphemy after Hamath and Samaria in v. 19.

Arminian close of the speech: they might yet have kept Jerusalem’s God uncompared. Historic claim at the wall, 8th century, is already named. The church is not to stretch “that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem” into a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: this insolence of ungodly men arises from their not understanding that God punishes the sins of men when they suffer any adversity. They venture to make a comparison between them and God himself. It is our duty to acknowledge that God inflicts punishment by the hand of wicked men, who may be regarded as the instruments of God’s anger. If wicked men are more powerful, let us not think that the arm of God is broken.

Reformed close of the speech: the comparison is still that historic theft of the Name at the wall. Calvin will not let “the LORD should deliver Jerusalem” pass as one more idol, nor as a later newspaper.

verses.text: But they were silent and answered him not a word, for the king's command was, “Do not answer him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley’s sending still holds: he sends Rabshakeh, who by his blasphemous persuasions tempts Hezekiah to despair, and the people to revolt. The people silent as the king commanded is still that temptation unmet after the speech of vv. 13–20.

Arminian reading: they might yet have held their peace because the king said so. Historic command at that wall is already named. The church is not to hunt another silence to make “do not answer him” a newspaper.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: ambassadors were sent to soothe the enemy; when they are unsuccessful they are enjoined to be silent, that they might not provoke that savage beast. It rather refers to those who guarded the walls, who, though they were sharply piqued by the taunts of the enemy, yet were not provoked to quarrels, because they obeyed the king’s command. It is no despicable courage, even when we have it not in our power to utter a syllable, still not to shrink or flinch, but to remain quietly in our place.

Reformed note: the silence is still that historic obedience at the wall. Calvin will not let “answered him not a word” become a newspaper of later crowds.

verses.text: Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and told him the words of the Rabshakeh.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: he sends Rabshakeh, who by his blasphemous persuasions tempts Hezekiah to despair, and the people to revolt. Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah with clothes torn are still that embassy bringing the wall-speech home, as in the Kings parallel.

Arminian close of the unit: they might yet have torn the clothes at that report. Historic household, secretary, and recorder, 8th century, are already named. The church is not to stretch “clothes torn” into a later headline.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: we now see that Eliakim and the other ambassadors were not silent as if they either approved of the impiety of Rabshakeh, or through dread of danger connived at such blasphemies; for they tear their garments. I except Shebna, who was destitute of piety, and was only driven by shame to assume the dress of mourning along with others as a matter of form.

Reformed close: the torn clothes are still that historic return from the wall. Calvin will not let the three look like one piety, nor turn the rending into a newspaper.
verses.keyContrast: Both keep the torn clothes as that historic return from the wall, not a newspaper and not a millennial camp fight. Wesley reads the three as the same embassy: Rabshakeh’s blasphemous persuasions tempt Hezekiah to despair and the people to revolt, and Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah come with clothes torn and tell the words. Calvin excepts Shebna: Eliakim and the others tear their garments as offended at the slanders; Shebna was destitute of piety, and was only driven by shame to assume the dress of mourning as a matter of form. Neither comment is an Arminian–Reformed millennial fight.
